In this March 16, 2022 statement, the Fed adopts a distinctly hawkish stance: strong labor markets coexist with elevated inflation driven by pandemic-era supply/demand imbalances and energy shocks, with the Russia–Ukraine war adding cost-push pressure and downside risks to growth. New Keynesian Phillips Curve insights and recent work on core non-tradable inflation suggest broadening price pressures and the risk that disinflation may require a prolonged period of above-neutral policy rates. Composition and weighting effects observed during COVID (e.g., the Israel “COVID-19 Inflation Weighting” study) caution that measured CPI can understate underlying pressures when consumption baskets shift, reinforcing the case for firming. “Inflation-at-risk” evidence (May 2024) indicates a skew toward upside inflation tails, consistent with the Committee’s signaling of “ongoing increases” and balance-sheet reduction. Taylor-rule benchmarks with low unemployment and high inflation would have supported a larger initial move; Bullard’s 50 bp dissent aligns with that literature and with Romer–Romer-style narratives that early decisive tightening can reduce longer-run costs. The plan to begin QT complements rate hikes via the term premium channel (consistent with term-structure findings and Goodfriend’s implementation emphasis on administered rates, ON RRP, and IOR). While average-inflation targeting from Jackson Hole 2020 allowed temporary overshoots, persistence of inflation and energy shocks now justify the pivot to faster normalization.

Overall, the tone is cautious and growth-negative but policy-confident on restoring price stability; relative to a neutral baseline, literature on upside inflation risks and supply-driven persistence tilts sentiment more negative than the prior assessment.
